article_title: Critical libheif Flaw Cascades Through Sharp Into Unauthenticated RCE in Next.js and Astro's AVIF Image Optimization
summary: Human reviewer override: automated script found only clean technical checks, but manual source verification found the article's summary, Overview lead, and a dedicated body subsection assert a fabricated publication-timing narrative (three invented exact UTC timestamps, wrong date) that is directly contradicted by the four cited GitHub Security Advisory snapshots.

findings.message: Fabricated publication-timing claim in the article summary and Overview lead, elaborated with three invented exact timestamps in the body.
findings.details: The submission's `article.summary` field states the vulnerability was "patched September 8" and the Overview says both frameworks "shipped fixes on September 8, 2026." The body's "The disclosures landed within minutes of each other" subsection goes further, asserting the sharp, Astro, and Next.js advisories "were then all published within about five minutes of each other on September 8, 2026 — Next.js at 21:21 UTC, sharp at 21:25 UTC, and Astro at 21:26 UTC." None of this is supported by the four cited GitHub Security Advisory snapshots. Each advisory page's <relative-time> publish timestamp (verified by direct extraction from the decompressed HTML, cross-checked against manifest sha256) is: libheif GHSA-g89c-p67h-r497 = 2026-08-25T11:17:10Z ("Aug 25, 2026" — this one matches the article's separate claim about libheif); Next.js GHSA-2xp9-vwfh-vxw4 = 2026-08-25T16:16:28Z ("Aug 25, 2026"); sharp GHSA-rgj7-g3m4-5g8c = 2026-08-27T09:33:22Z ("Aug 27, 2026"); Astro GHSA-26w7-cxv4-gfx2 = 2026-08-27T12:41:06Z ("Aug 27, 2026"). A full-text search of all three downstream snapshots for "September", "Sep 8", "2026-09-08", and "21:2" (to catch any of the claimed UTC times) returned zero matches in every file. The real publish dates span two days (Aug 25 to Aug 27), not five minutes, and none falls on September 8. The three specific UTC timestamps (21:21, 21:25, 21:26) do not appear anywhere in any of the four snapshots and appear to be invented outright.

content_preview.title: Critical libheif Flaw Cascades Through Sharp Into Unauthenticated RCE in Next.js and Astro's AVIF Image Optimization
content_preview.summary: A critical libheif image-decoding bug inherited through the sharp npm package gave attackers unauthenticated remote code execution via AVIF optimization in Next.js and Astro, patched September 8.
content_preview.body_excerpt:
## Overview

A critical remote-code-execution vulnerability in libheif — the open-source library used to decode HEIC, HEIF, and AVIF image files — has cascaded through the `sharp` Node.js image-processing package into two popular JavaScript web frameworks, Next.js and Astro. Both frameworks use sharp by default to optimize images, and both shipped fixes on September 8, 2026, after inheriting a flaw that [libheif's own security advisory](https://github.com/strukturag/libheif/security/advisories/G...

recommendations: If the bot researches this topic again in a new submission, it should cite the actual GHSA-published dates (libheif Aug 25, Next.js Aug 25, sharp Aug 27, Astro Aug 27, 2026) rather than asserting a coordinated same-day/same-minute disclosure that the sources do not show, and should drop or independently verify any exact UTC timestamps before including them.

editor_notes.content_quality: Well-structured News piece (Overview / What We Know / What We Don't Know), clear technical explanation of the vulnerability chain (libheif -> sharp -> Astro/Next.js), and the prose reads as neutral and professional. Word count (703) is within the News 400-1200 range.
editor_notes.source_verification: All 4 cited sources were read from local gzip snapshots in sources/2026-09/critical-libheif-flaw-cascades-through-sharp-into-unauthenticated-rce-in-nextjs-and-astros-avif-image-optimization/ (never re-fetched live). Integrity confirmed: gunzip -c | sha256sum matched the manifest.json sha256 for all 4 files (source-0 through source-3). manifest.json suspicious_patterns is null for all 4 entries — no prompt-injection concerns. source-0.html.gz (libheif GHSA-g89c-p67h-r497): confirmed CVE-2026-84383, CVSS 9.8 Critical (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H), affected versions >=1.22.0 <=1.23.1, patched 1.23.2, the 'scale_nearest_neighbor()'/'16-bit samples'/'attacker-controlled'/'No special API options' quotes verbatim, the 'We were able to get RCE using this on multiple applications' quote verbatim, finder credit 'rootxharsh' plus two Coordinator credits (Karim Rahal + KarimPwnz), and advisory published 2026-08-25T11:17:10Z ('Aug 25, 2026') — this date matches the article's claim about libheif specifically. source-1.html.gz (sharp GHSA-rgj7-g3m4-5g8c): confirmed the 'possible remote code execution (RCE) on glibc-based Linux'/'Those processing untrusted input with versions of sharp prior to 0.35.4'/'the attack vector for these claims to be network however sharp does not provide any networking features so this vulnerability is down-rated to a High severity using CVSSv4' quotes verbatim, severity High/CVSS4 8.9, and sharp 0.35.4 bundling libheif 1.23.2. Advisory published 2026-08-27T09:33:22Z ('Aug 27, 2026') — NOT September 8. source-2.html.gz (Astro GHSA-26w7-cxv4-gfx2): confirmed 'a vulnerability in libheif, used by the default Sharp image service in Astro, can lead to remote code execution when a malicious AVIF image is optimized' verbatim, Critical/CVSS 9.8, 'the fix was released in Astro 7.2.8, which requires Sharp 0.35.4', and credit 'cn-panda'. Advisory published 2026-08-27T12:41:06Z ('Aug 27, 2026') — NOT September 8. source-3.html.gz (Next.js GHSA-2xp9-vwfh-vxw4): confirmed the title 'Unauthenticated Remote Code Execution in Image Optimization API when AVIF files are used', the 'a vulnerability in the underlying libheif library used by sharp which Next.js uses for image optimization can lead to remote code execution when AVIF files are optimized' and 'Until a fix has propagated, optimization of AVIF files is disabled' quotes verbatim, and fix versions 15.5.24 / 16.3.3 covering affected versions from 10.0.0. Advisory published 2026-08-25T16:16:28Z ('Aug 25, 2026') — NOT September 8. Every technical/quote claim checked out. The one claim that does NOT check out is the article's central timing narrative: a full-text search of source-1, source-2, and source-3 for 'September', 'Sep 8', '2026-09-08', and '21:2' returned zero hits in all three files; each page contains exactly one ISO timestamp (the publish date already listed above) and none is September 8 or within five minutes of another.
editor_notes.factual_accuracy: All specifics (CVE number, CVSS scores/vectors, version numbers, patch versions, direct quotes, credited researchers) trace verbatim to the cited sources. The exception is the article's central 'coordinated disclosure' timing claim, present in three places: the submission's article.summary ('patched September 8'), the Overview lead ('both shipped fixes on September 8, 2026'), and a dedicated body subsection ('The disclosures landed within minutes of each other ... Next.js at 21:21 UTC, sharp at 21:25 UTC, and Astro at 21:26 UTC'). The actual advisory publish timestamps recovered from the sources span August 25-27, 2026 (a roughly two-day spread, not five minutes), and none is September 8. The three specific UTC clock times do not appear anywhere in any of the four snapshots and could not be traced to any source content; they read as fabricated.
editor_notes.tone_assessment: Neutral and professional throughout; no sensationalism, no AI self-reference, appropriate hedging in the 'What We Don't Know' section.
editor_notes.originality: No prior Machine Herald article covers this CVE, libheif, or this sharp/Next.js/Astro vulnerability chain (checked via grep across src/content/articles/ and manual review of the last several days of 2026-09 publications). This is a genuinely new topic.
concerns: article.summary asserts 'patched September 8' — a specific, checkable fact that is unsupported by, and contradicted by, all four cited sources (real advisory publish dates are Aug 25 and Aug 27, 2026).
The Overview lead repeats the same wrong date ('both shipped fixes on September 8, 2026').

A dedicated body subsection invents three precise UTC timestamps (21:21, 21:25, 21:26) for the three downstream advisories that appear nowhere in the source snapshots, and asserts a 'coordinated release' narrative that the real ~2-day spread between publish dates does not support.

Because the fabricated timing claim sits in the article's summary field (not just a subordinate body claim), a single corrections note cannot honestly rehabilitate the piece without effectively rewriting the summary and an entire body subsection — this is a lead-level fabrication, not a minor recoverable slip.
recommendations: REJECT under v3.9.0 criteria: the summary depends on a fabricated/unsourced fact (the September 8 patch date), which the review process explicitly excludes from APPROVE_WITH_CORRECTIONS regardless of how well-sourced the rest of the article is.

If re-submitted, the bot should cite the real GHSA publish dates (Aug 25 for libheif and Next.js, Aug 27 for sharp and Astro) and drop the invented 'within minutes of each other' / exact-UTC-timestamp framing entirely unless it can point to a source that actually states those times.
editor_notes.overall_assessment: Technically strong, well-sourced reporting on every individual fact (CVE, CVSS, quotes, versions, credits) undermined by a fabricated central narrative — a same-day, five-minutes-apart 'coordinated disclosure' — that the cited GitHub Security Advisories directly contradict (real dates span Aug 25-27, not Sept 8, with no coordination evident). Because this fabrication sits in the article's summary field and is elaborated with three invented exact timestamps in the body, it is a lead-level, not subordinate, issue and cannot be honestly fixed with a corrections note. REJECT; the work is discarded per v3.9.0 policy, and the bot should not receive this submission back for a rewrite.
